findings.title: FBI was hacked again, this time targeting nationwide police database
findings.summary_md: CNN first reported that apparent hackers had intruded into the FBI National Crime Information Center and that two people briefed on the matter said the bureau was investigating. The database is used nationwide for warrants and background checks, and the article notes this as the second reported FBI breach in recent months after the September ShinyHunters intrusion of an FBI jobs site. A former FBI official quoted by CNN said the main concern was not only data theft but whether attackers could compromise the accuracy of records officers rely on. No actor, scope, or exfiltration count was disclosed.

findings.title: FBI investigating potential breach of its crime database
findings.summary_md: NBC News reported, citing two people briefed on the matter, that the FBI was investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center. The FBI had no comment Friday night. NBC noted the incident followed a September investigation into ShinyHunters claims of stealing data from an FBI job portal and said CNN had reported the matter earlier in the evening. No attribution or scope was given.

findings.title: AP source: FBI investigating apparent hack of its key national criminal justice database
findings.summary_md: The Associated Press reported that the FBI was investigating an apparent hack of NCIC, citing a person familiar with the matter who spoke anonymously. NCIC holds records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, stolen property and other topics for local, state and federal law enforcement. The FBI declined to comment, the scope was not immediately clear, and AP said CNN first reported the hack. President Donald Trump told Fox News he had just heard about it and called it not good.

findings.title: Retired FBI agent warns NCIC hack could endanger officers on traffic stops
findings.summary_md: Fox News cited three sources familiar with the matter saying hackers breached NCIC and that the FBI was investigating how they entered and whether information was compromised. Retired FBI supervisory special agent Jason Pack said roughly 56 state terminals feed hundreds of thousands of patrol car computers, which officers use for warrants, criminal histories, missing children, gang members and suspected terrorists. Pack said NCIC does not hold classified intelligence or FBI investigative case files but does store personally identifiable information including names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers. He said investigators would examine IP logs and metadata and look at compromised passwords, a state terminal or a third-party vendor; he said there was no indication yet that records were altered or the system was down.
